# 17-expanse — sources

Back-test entry `17-expanse.yaml`: Expanse, job sizes predicted at submit time on shared GPU clusters (YC Spring 2026,
P26). Written 2026-10-22 from public material only, read that day. Quotes are verbatim from the page named. "Author's
choice" marks the smallest plausible choice made where the public material is silent. The launch era is the Launch YC
post of 2026-05-04 and the Launch HN of 2026-06-01 (the founder's gap-11 rule: every figure pinned to the launch era
where one exists; anything later is marked as later and sits under *Status today*).

Main sources (short names used below):
- [LYC] Launch YC: "Expanse - Unlock wasted GPU capacity", 2026-05-04 (created_at in the page data) — https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/QCF-expanse-unlock-wasted-gpu-capacity
- [HN] Launch HN: "Launch HN: Expanse (YC P26) – Unlock Wasted GPU Capacity", 2026-06-01, the founders' post and the thread (27 comments), read whole through the HN Algolia API — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48356312 (https://hn.algolia.com/api/v1/items/48356312)
- [WB] expanse.sh as archived 2026-06-01, the day of the Launch HN — https://web.archive.org/web/20260601142950/https://expanse.sh/
- [YCP] YC company page, read 2026-10-22 — https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/expanse
- [SITE] expanse.sh, read 2026-10-22 — https://expanse.sh

## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** Researchers and ML engineers who submit jobs to a shared SLURM or Kubernetes GPU cluster.
   [LYC] "Running compute on a cluster means guessing memory, time, and GPUs before you submit."
   [HN] "We also flag failures we think are about to happen and surface line-level optimisations the researcher can apply
   themselves." → `roles[researcher]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`.

2. **What (the job).** Get each job to run to the end without wasting the cluster.
   [LYC] "Get it wrong and your job fails mid-run. Over-guess and you pay for compute you never use."
   [HN] "under-requesting kills your job mid-run and you lose days of work. So everyone over-requests by two to three
   times." → `statements.problem`, `context.job`, `interpretations.problem`.

3. **When / where.** At every job submission. [HN] "We scan any workloads about to be submitted through SLURM/K8s
   (plugging into the life cycles of the job so you don't have to change how you submit things)". → `context.circumstance`,
   `occasion: job submission`. Author's choice: the window {5, WORKING_DAYS} (several submissions a working day) and
   Frequency 3 to 5 working days out of 5; Prevalence `p_80_100` ("everyone over-requests").

4. **Which people.** Researchers on SLURM or Kubernetes clusters of 100 or more GPUs, at national HPC centres, AI labs,
   quant funds and drug discovery.
   [HN] "If you run a HPC/GPU cluster (SLURM or K8s, 100+ GPUs), we'd love to have a talk." [LYC] "Know anyone in AI
   infrastructure (managing cloud and/or on-premise data centres), quant finance, drug discovery, or AI research labs?"
   → `context.segment`, `market: US`. Author's choice: US (rule U); the founders are in Edinburgh and the cluster they
   measured is a national-scale HPC site, and their ask names no country.

5. **Who pays.** The cluster's operator, per cluster; a department runs the paid pilot.
   [HN] "We offer a two-week measurement window where we install, ingest, and report recoverable capacity to datacenter
   operators, followed by a paid pilot deployment in one department at a fixed monthly fee, renewing at the same rate
   unless the scope expands." → `persona.decision_maker: {role: operator}`; Buyer and payer tests "The department head"
   (the author's reading of "in one department"), "The security team" listed. Purchase friction's tested item, "A security
   review of an agent on every node", from [HN] "Expanse installs on every node" and the thread's security objection
   ("Any competent enterprise risk team is going to give a hard no to a SaaS application being in the critical path for
   on-prem business critical workloads.") with the founder's reply ("Deployments are air-gapped and run in the customer's
   VPC, on their own hardware."); "Letting it read job scripts and source code" from [HN] "We read the source code, job
   submission script, and the hardware"; the budget line for the department's pilot is the author's. Commitment's step,
   "run a two-week waste measurement on the cluster": [WB] "Two weeks on your cluster. A real wastage number. No
   commitment. If the numbers don't justify a pilot, you walk away with the report." (The same post also offers "a
   section of your cluster for a week"; the two weeks of the pricing paragraph and the site are used.)

6. **Mechanism.** An agent on every node, hooked into the scheduler; a cluster-specific model predicts what each job needs
   at submit time.
   [HN] "Expanse installs on every node and hooks into SLURM (or the K8s scheduler). It ingests live hardware telemetry
   (DCGM, CUPTI, Cgroups, Network/IO monitoring)". [HN] "We predict the GPU VRAM, Utilisation, memory, CPUs and walltime
   the job actually needs, with a confidence interval." [HN] "If a workload fails, we take all the data we collected and
   perform correlations on the stack profiling and the hardware telemetry". [LYC] "All analysis runs on your network."
   → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`. Compatibility: the source code on the cluster beside the script
   (tested; the model reads it), the usual scheduler, Python ([HN] "currently only supported in python - other languages
   coming soon", of the profiler) — the conditions are the author's from these lines. Adoption friction: using the
   suggested sizes instead of padding (tested; [HN] "Our models are trained to over-provision rather than
   under-provision"), applying the code fixes. Relative advantage: [LYC] "Debug failures in seconds, not days"
   (fewer_attempts, the job runs first time) and a shorter queue wait for smaller requests (shorter_time, the author's
   reading of a smaller request fitting sooner); the wording is the author's.

7. **Price and cost.** Per cluster a month, no figure; the cost is the share of the cluster's GPU hours reserved and
   never used.
   [HN] "We're currently onboarding customers as paid pilots. Pricing is determined per-cluster." No figure exists in
   [LYC], [HN], [WB] or [SITE] (no pricing page). The founder's price, AMOUNT_PERIOD **$10,000 to $20,000 per cluster a
   month**, is the operator's reading: for the smallest cluster the founders address (100 GPUs, about 73,000 GPU hours a
   month), [LYC]'s 30% reserved and unused is about 22,000 GPU hours, which at an assumed $2 to $3 a GPU hour (the
   author's assumption; [HN] prices its $8.5M "At on-demand cloud rates for the same hardware" without naming a rate) is
   about $44,000 to $66,000 a month; a fee of a fifth to a third of the waste on the smallest cluster is the author's
   choice. Existing sacrifice: RATE, about 30% to 59% of the cluster's GPU hours per cluster a month, the low from [LYC],
   the high from [HN]'s measured cluster. Ability to pay is read `budget` by the engine (a percent never compares with
   dollars), so the operators answer the registry's budget question.

8. **Occasions.** The stories are scripted from the thread; no respondent is a real person.
   [HN] (a genomics user) "I do genomics work and my jobs tend to be bursty. They may use a lot of CPU initially, but the
   second half of the job is writing results. This takes only one core, but still the max amount of memory." [HN] (an
   HPC user) "I know from snooping on sumbit scripts and node utilization on the HPC that I use at my institution that
   most submissions leave some compute on the table (and many of them are egregiously bad)." [HN] (a student) "It's not
   trivial to estimate a priori the amount of time required for my simulation to complete, so I overestimate."

## Respondents → the public account each is based on

Researchers (PRIMARY link, Parts 1 and 2):
- Priyanka Raghunathan → [HN] "under-requesting kills your job mid-run and you lose days of work"; the fine-tuning run is the author's.
- Tobias Brandt → [HN] the genomics comment (bursty pipeline, "about 8 different steps", "We need to reserve the $MAX requirements for each").
- Ana Lucía Ferreira → [HN] the student's "so I overestimate" on simulation time; the queue wait for a big request is the author's.
- Kwabena Owusu → author's invention, filling a gap: an ML engineer whose sizes come from past runs on a dashboard, so the problem is not a chorus (against on Importance and Current solution).
- Mei-Ling Zhou → author's invention: a chipped (rather_not_say) story at a quant fund, GUESSED by code.
- Rafael Moreno → author's invention: a vague, habitual story (GUESSED), echoing [HN] "everyone over-requests by two to three times".
- Ingrid Haugen → author's invention: a gate No (writing up, no jobs that week).
- Samuel Adeyemi → author's invention: a gate No (away at a conference).
- Yusuf Demir → [HN] "snooping on sumbit scripts ... many of them are egregiously bad": a copied script holding eight GPUs.
- Claire Dubois-Martin → author's invention, filling a gap: a licensed binary with no source code, so the tested condition fails ('no').
- Hiroshi Takeda → [HN] "at least for everyone else, I'd would prefer tuning my own usage myself": he profiles a test run (Current solution mostly works; Adoption friction no).
- Fatima Al-Sayed → [HN] "you lose days of work"; the walltime limit and the group allocation are the author's.
- Diego Castañeda → [HN] the student's PDE simulation ("If I'm running a PDE simulation, and I allocate n machines I want to use all of them"); he keeps his margin (Adoption friction probably not).

Cluster operators (COMMERCIAL_B2B link, Part 3 only; no story by rule). Their picks are the author's, shaped by:
- Gregory Lindqvist, Nadia Kowalski, Marco Bianchi → [HN] the measured national cluster and "Datacenters run at roughly 30% to 40% effective utilisation": operators who see the waste and would pay at the founder's band.
- Arjun Mehta → [HN] "large scale compute industries as well, such as quant funds": a quant-fund platform lead who owns the compute budget, sees more waste than the founder's high and decides alone (against the tested department head).
- Beatrix Okoro → [HN] "What you are really left with is the 'small and medium business' clusters that are purpose specific": a small cluster, less waste, a lower rung.
- Thomas Reinholt → [HN] the security objection ("a hard no"); would not pay.
- Leilani Kahale → [HN] "In many places the cost of the HPC hardware isn't passed onto them": a grant-funded university cluster that does not measure the waste (dont_know) and has no line for a monthly fee.

The split (4 of 7 operators at the founder's rung or above; 5 of 6 who give a number at 30% waste or more) is the
author's reading of a thread that agreed on the waste and argued about security and the business. No respondent
carries the name of a commenter, customer or founder.

## Status today

Same idea, five months after launch. [SITE] "Expanse delivers compute certainty. We predict exactly what every job
needs before it runs", still sales-led ("Book a discovery call"), now citing "$8M Monthly wastage uncovered" (a later
figure, not used). [YCP] lists the company as Spring 2026 with the Launch YC text. No public price today ([SITE] has no
pricing page, read 2026-10-22).

## Could not be sourced

- **A price figure.** None at launch or today; the founder's $10,000 to $20,000 per cluster a month is the operator's
  (author's) reading, and the GPU-hour rate behind its arithmetic is an assumption.
- **The waste per cluster as an operator would read it.** The founders' 30% is an industry figure they cite and their
  59% is one national cluster; the operators' value boxes (20% to 60%) are the author's.
- **A buyer title and who has to agree.** [HN] names "datacenter operators" and "one department"; the decider role, the
  department head as the tested role and the security team are the author's reading.
- **A US market.** The founders are in Edinburgh; the US is the author's choice under rule U.
- **A researcher's hour.** No source; `hourly_rate` 60 is a round stand-in, unread by the RATE cost.
- The Compatibility and Adoption friction conditions, the Purchase friction items but the security review, and every
  pick are the author's.

insights.line: What would make it worth more?

whys.g1: The three answers raise distinct concerns (needing proof of waste from our own cluster, a security veto on node agents, and grant-funded budgets that can't absorb a monthly fee), so leaving each on its own is how a cluster operator would read them; there is no shared group any of them was wrongly kept out of.
whys.g2: There is no junk, explicit or off-topic answer on this line, and none is grouped.

founder.order_why: The flow follows my own pitch: the researcher's submit-time guess, the scheduler-hooked prediction, then the operator who pays per cluster, so I never had to answer about the buyer before the problem was set.
founder.asked_twice: Screen 20 (first real step) and screen 22 (Offer a pilot?): my first step is the free two-week measurement that leads into the paid pilot, so the pilot offer repeats what I had already said at 20.

COMMERCIAL_B2B.order_why: The 'One more thing' screen on what would take the time in buying sits between 5 of 6 and 6 of 6, interrupting the run, and it would fit better after the security-review question or at the very end.
COMMERCIAL_B2B.asked_twice: Screen 7 (what would take the time in buying) largely re-asks screens 5 and 6, since sign-off and the security review are exactly what would take the time.
COMMERCIAL_B2B.missing: What I already use to see reserved-but-unused GPU hours (scheduler accounting, Grafana or vendor tools) and why it isn't enough; whether the cluster runs SLURM or Kubernetes and how big it is; and whether the researchers would accept being told their memory, GPU and time requests are wrong.

screens.why4: It is a free-text box with a 'Nobody is an answer' hint and one escape chip, 'Leave this out of the study', which fits a founder who has not pinned down the approvers.
screens.why5: I typed the department head and the security team, but Keel's belief keeps only the department head and drops the security review, which is the objection I most expect.
screens.instead: Besides the cluster operator, who has to agree before they can buy? (belief: The cluster operator decides; the department head and the security team have to agree.)

screens.why1: Right after I named who else has to agree, it is natural to check the list of people Keel will test before it goes to strangers.
screens.why2: Researcher, cluster operator, department head and security team are exactly the words my trade uses for who touches a cluster purchase.
screens.why3: I know who sits around a cluster deal: the researcher who submits jobs, the operator who buys, the department running the pilot and the security team reviewing an agent on every node.
screens.why4: The first two rows carry a part ('has the problem', 'decides to buy') but the department head and the security team carry none, and the casing is uneven ('researcher', 'Cluster operator', 'The department head'), so I can't see that the security team is listed but not the one being tested.
screens.why5: It keeps my roles and my reading: the operator decides, the department head running the pilot has to agree, and the security team is listed beside them without being tested.
screens.instead: Rows: Researcher · has the problem; Cluster operator · decides to buy; Department head · has to agree; Security team · also involved

screens.why1: Right after I named the department head and the security team as the people who have to agree, it is obvious that I now pick the one to test, and I would pick the department head who signs the pilot budget.
screens.why2: The list is plain, but the bar reads 'the last time they bought stop guessing memory, time and GPUs', which is not grammatical, so I have to read it twice to see it means a job-sizing tool.
screens.why3: Who signs off on a per-cluster fee is my own reading of how my pilots get bought, so I can answer it straight away.
screens.why4: The two roles I typed plus 'Nobody else' (the operator decides alone) cover every belief I hold, they are distinct, and they use my words.
screens.why5: The belief keeps my operator and department head, but the bar names the purchase as 'stop guessing memory, time and GPUs', which is a benefit and not something an operator has ever bought, so it drifts from what I sell.
screens.instead: Same list (The department head / The security team / Nobody else), with the bar reading: Holds if at least 2 in 3 cluster operators say the department head had to agree the last time they bought a tool or service for their cluster.

screens.why1: After who has to agree, asking what could slow or stop the purchase is the obvious next step of how it sells, and for an agent on every node it is the question I most need tested.
screens.why2: Approvals, security review, procurement and an agent on every node are the words a founder selling into HPC and cluster operations uses every day.
screens.why3: I know from every discovery call that the security review of a node agent, the access to job scripts and source code, and the pilot's budget line are what stall us.
screens.why4: The only option shown is the escape chip, which fits a free-text answer that the next screen checks.
screens.why5: The belief keeps my first item, the security review, but it adds a 6-week bound I never typed and drops the source-code access and the budget line, so the meaning has drifted a little.
screens.instead: Keep the question; have the belief name the security review of a node agent that reads job scripts and source code, without a time bound I never gave.

screens.why1: Right after I named what could slow a purchase, Keel shows the list back for me to check, which is where a check belongs.
screens.why2: An agent on every node, job scripts, a budget line for a pilot and a vendor agreement are how my trade and my buyers talk, readable on first pass.
screens.why3: These are the hurdles I hit in every operator conversation, the security objection above all, so I know them first-hand.
screens.why4: The four rows are distinct and cover the real path: security sign-off, data access to scripts and code, money for the pilot, and paperwork, all under nine words.
screens.why5: The security review of a per-node agent stays my tested item, and the belief's 'or not need it' leaves room for my air-gapped, in-VPC answer without changing what I typed.

screens.why1: Right after I listed what could slow a purchase and checked Keel's wording, picking the one step to put a time on is the obvious next move, and the security review is the one I know will bite.
screens.why2: "If they bought it, how long would this step take before it went through" is a little circular, since the review happens before the buy, so I read it twice before landing on "how long until security signs off"; the rest is plain ops language to me.
screens.why3: I have sat through enough enterprise and HPC-centre security reviews of node agents to put a weeks figure on it from my own pipeline.
screens.why4: The four are my own items and the days/weeks/months unit menu fits, but "letting it read job scripts and source code" is really part of the same security review rather than a separate step with its own clock, so two of them overlap.
screens.why5: The belief says what I meant: operators clear a security review of a per-node agent within about six weeks, or skip it because the deployment is air-gapped on their own hardware.
screens.instead: Before your organisation could run a tool that puts an agent on every node of your cluster, how long would its security review take? (days / weeks / months, or: we would not need one)

screens.why1: After who decides, what it costs, the price and what slows a purchase, asking what first real step I want the operator to take is the obvious last commercial question, and it is where my two-week measurement belongs.
screens.why2: The question is plain, and the hint's 'time, data, money or a signature' tells me straight away that letting an agent on every node read telemetry for two weeks counts as a real step.
screens.why3: It asks about my own sales motion, and I know my first step exactly: two weeks on their cluster, a real wastage number, then a paid pilot or they walk away.
screens.why4: The only option is the free-text box with a 'Leave this out of the study' chip, and that escape fits a founder who has no step to test.
screens.why5: The belief Keel wrote, that the cluster operator would run a two-week waste measurement on the cluster, keeps my words and my buyer; the trailing 'now' is harmless.

screens.why1: After I named the first step on the previous screen, it is obvious to check how Keel cut it down for strangers before the commercial frame closes.
screens.why2: A cluster operator reads 'a two-week waste measurement on the cluster' on first pass; waste, cluster and measurement are their own words.
screens.why3: Whether to let a vendor measure waste on their own cluster for two weeks is exactly the operator's call, and they know their answer.
screens.why4: The screen shows my step as Keel wrote it and the test with its bar, with no options, chips or value box to judge.
screens.why5: Keel dropped the 'free' and 'no commitment' from my offer, and 'the operator would run' makes it sound like their team does the work, when we install, ingest and report; both change what a stranger says yes to.
screens.instead: Let us measure your cluster's waste for two weeks, free (8 words), tested as: in most cases the cluster operator would let Expanse run a free two-week waste measurement on the cluster now.

screens.why1: Just before the study goes out is the obvious point to decide whether strangers get asked to take a real step, and it follows directly from the commitment step I set on the previous screens.
screens.why2: It is short and clear, but in my trade a 'pilot' is the paid department deployment that comes after the free two-week measurement, so 'Offer a pilot?' makes me read twice to see that it only means collecting emails.
screens.why3: Whether I want to follow up with people who say yes is my own call, and it is easy to answer.
screens.why4: Yes or no covers it, the two options are distinct, and no escape chip is needed for a founder's own choice.
screens.why5: The line shown, 'Would you try this for real? Leave your email.', drops the step I typed, a two-week waste measurement on the cluster, and is generic enough that a researcher who cannot install anything on the cluster could still say yes.
screens.instead: Ask the people who say they'd pay to leave an email for the step you set? They'll see: "Would you run a free two-week waste measurement on your cluster? Leave your email." — Yes, ask them / No, don't ask

screens.why1: Choosing who asks the researchers is the natural last setup step before the link goes out, and nothing earlier asked it.

screens.why3: It is my own choice as the founder, and I can make it by hearing each 5-second sample.

screens.why5: It keeps 'researchers' and leaks nothing, but what I picked was the preselected face, while the screen calls the choice a voice, so the video interviewer drifts a little between face and voice.
screens.instead: Who should ask researchers your questions on video? (Daphne, picked for you / Saskia; tap to hear each.) Hint: whichever you pick is used for every interview in this project, 400 credits either way; people can read and type instead of talking.

screens.why1: Right after choosing who asks the researchers, it is obvious I now pick how the cluster operators, who only get the pricing part, will answer.
screens.why2: 'How should operators answer?' is plain to me, and the three modes (talk to an AI on video, read and tap, or let them pick) read clearly on first pass despite the doubled 'Daphne Daphne' label.
screens.why3: I know my operators are busy, security-minded infra people who would rather tap through a short form than talk to a recorded AI, so I can answer this from what I know.
screens.why4: The three options are complete and distinct, and each carries its readiness status, so nothing is missing or overlapping.
screens.why5: It keeps my operators as the second audience and adds nothing of the product or roles that would leak to them.

screens.why1: Choosing who gets the link is the obvious last step once the operators' answer mode is set, so it belongs here at the end of the flow.
screens.why2: The choice itself is plain, but 'from a search on the Contacts page' names a part of Keel I have not seen in this flow, so I would read that option twice.
screens.why3: I know who I am sending to: the operators of 100+ GPU clusters I have met by name, plus researchers I could reach where they already talk.
screens.why4: The three ways are distinct, but there is no way to send researchers one way and operators another, and my study has both groups.
screens.why5: The screen never says whether the link is for the researchers or the cluster operators, though my study asks the two groups different parts.
screens.instead: Who gets a link, for each group? Researchers: people I know by name / a list from Keel's contacts / one open link I post where they are (an HPC or SLURM users' channel). Cluster operators: the same three choices.

screens.why_b1: "Did not hold" sits right under the title with the deciding number beside it (Purchase friction: 4 of 7 expect longer than 6 weeks against a bar of no more than 2 of 7), so I know the money stage fails and which card sank it.
screens.why_b2: Each card shows what is counted, over how many and where my bar sits ("5 of 7 said yes · bar 5 of 7 · at the bar"), though Existing sacrifice's 6 rather than 7 is not explained here.
screens.why_b3: Buyer and payer, Purchase friction and Commitment carry my lines word for word, and the other three cards use my own figures ($10,000 to $20,000 per cluster a month, 30% to 59% of GPU hours).
screens.why_b4: The page tells me the stage failed but not what to do about it: nothing about planning sales around a 6-week-to-3-month security review, leading with the air-gapped, in-VPC deployment, or testing a lower price rung.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible and the at-the-bar holds are marked as such, but Price at 4 of 7 against a bar of 5 is softened to "People disagree" instead of being called short, and nowhere does the page say that 7 operators is a thin base.
screens.instead: Did not hold: 4 of 7 operators expect the security review to run past 6 weeks (most often 6 weeks to 3 months), so plan pilots for a quarter-long review and lead with the air-gapped deployment; price is also 1 short of your bar, and Commitment and Buyer and payer only just hold at 5 of 7.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right beside its deciding count, 5 of 6 at 30% or more against a bar of 4 of 6, so I know it held and by how much.

screens.why_b3: It is my existing-sacrifice figure, 30% to 59% of the cluster's GPU hours reserved and never used, in my words, though "of the cluster's GPU hours per cluster a month" says cluster twice.
screens.why_b4: It tells me the waste is real for these operators and that the open question is whether they will pay to remove it, pointing me to the Price card next.
screens.why_b5: The screen keeps n visible (7 answered, 6 counted), names Leilani as not counted and why, and calls it "a lean, not a call", so "the cost is there" is held in check.
screens.instead: Mark my 30–59% band on the percent axis and put the 4-of-6 bar on the people strip, so the range and the head count don't share one line; say "You said" once.

screens.why_b1: The status 'People disagree' sits right beside 4 of 7 at $10,000 or more against a bar of 5 of 7, one short, so I know my price belief fell just short and by how much.
screens.why_b2: The buckets count operators by what they would pay a month per cluster, all 7 are on it, my band is marked in the $10,000 to $25,000 bucket, and the strip puts the bar at 5 of 7, all on first look.
screens.why_b3: Price, worth $10,000 to $20,000 per cluster a month, is my band in my per-cluster, per-month terms.
screens.why_b4: The So line only says I'm one short and sends me to the Insights tab, though the quotes beside it already show three different reasons I'd act on differently: a small cluster wants to see its own report, a security veto that no price fixes, and grant money with no monthly line.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible, it says 'a lean, not a call', and it doesn't oversell 4 of 7; calling the would-not-pay 'short of it' is a little loose but not misleading.
screens.instead: 4 of 7 at my band, one short; of the 3 against, one is a security no that price won't fix, one would move after seeing their own two-week report, one has grant money and no monthly line, so lead with the free measurement and offer grant-aligned annual billing before I cut the price.

screens.why_b1: Too few to call sits beside 4 of 7 named your price · 5 needed, but the chart shows 3 of 4 meeting my bar, so the number beside the verdict and the chart point different ways.
screens.why_b2: The four answers and the bar at 3 of 4 are plain, but the strip draws a fifth ghost cell while the count line says 4 answered and 4 counted, and I had to look twice to see what it stands for.
screens.why_b3: I recognise my price band and my operators in the belief line, but I never wrote this belief; Keel derived it from my price.
screens.why_b4: Waits until 5 have cannot happen, since only 4 named my price and everyone has answered, so it never says what to do, such as asking more operators at my price.
screens.why_b5: n is visible throughout, the small group is called a lean, not a call, and 3 of 4 is not claimed as a hold.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right beside 5 of 7 against a bar of 5 of 7, marked "at the bar", so I know it held and by exactly how much.
screens.why_b2: Four answer bars, each marked for or against, a strip of 7 cells with the marker at 5, and the count line saying 7 answered and 7 counted: what is counted, over whom and where the bar sits are all plain on first look.
screens.why_b3: The title is Buyer and payer and the line is word for word the belief I checked: the cluster operator decides, and the department head has to agree.
screens.why_b4: "Plan for the department head in most deals" is a concrete instruction for how I run the pilot sale, and it notes the one operator who could sign alone.

screens.why_b1: "Did not hold" sits right beside 4 of 7 expecting longer than 6 weeks against a bar of no more than 2 of 7, so I see both the verdict and the number that decides it.

screens.why_b1: 'Holding up' sits right beside '5 of 7 said yes · bar 5 of 7 · at the bar', so I see the verdict and the number that decides it together.

screens.why_b1: Both boxes open on their verdict (People disagree, Did not hold) with the deciding count and bar beside it: 4 of 7 against a bar of 5 of 7 for price, and 4 of 7 against a ceiling of 2 of 7 for the review time.
screens.why_b3: Both belief lines are the ones I checked: the $10,000 to $20,000 per cluster a month, and the security review of an agent on every node within about 6 weeks.
screens.why_b4: Nothing on the screen says what to do next; the quotes point at three moves (an air-gapped security pack, grant-term pricing, leading with the two-week report for small clusters), but I have to draw them out myself.

screens.why_b6: The price quotes add things I did not type: grant-funded clusters have no line for a monthly fee, small clusters recover only a few nodes, and security is a refusal at any price rather than a delay.

screens.why1: As the first screen on the buying-decision link, showing me the idea before asking whether I'd buy it is exactly where it belongs.
screens.why2: SLURM, Kubernetes, GPU memory and walltime are my daily words, but 'predicted job resource needs' is a clumsy label and 'line-level optimisations' and 'hooks into on every node' would make me reread to work out whether it is an agent on my compute nodes.
screens.why3: I run the cluster and watch jobs over-request and fail, so I can judge this from what I see every week.
screens.why4: A card to read with no options shown.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's what and when, but the first line names a feature rather than saying what it is, and 'your researchers submit' casts me as their manager in a way that sounds like the founder's framing.
screens.why6: Heard once, the semicolon in 'Your researchers submit; it reads...' and the four-item list 'GPU memory, memory, CPUs and walltime' are a mouthful, and 'memory' right after 'GPU memory' sounds like a slip.
screens.instead: Imagine Expanse, a tool that predicts what each job on your cluster needs. It runs on your own network alongside SLURM or Kubernetes and checks each job as researchers submit it. It estimates GPU memory, system memory, CPUs and run time, warns of likely failures, and suggests code fixes. When a job fails, it says why and how to fix it. The people building it believe it would be used on every job at submit time, and again whenever one fails.

screens.why1: Right after the idea card, asking how much of my cluster was wasted is the obvious first thing to establish about the cost I live with today.
screens.why2: "Reserve and never use" isn't how I'd put it; I'd have to stop and decide whether you mean allocated GPUs sitting idle, or requested walltime the job never reached, because sacct and my dashboards report those separately.
screens.why3: I can pull allocated-versus-used GPU hours from accounting, but off the top of my head on a phone I'd be giving a rough figure from the last utilisation report rather than last month's exact number.
screens.why4: A percent box suits it, but "None" sits beside "I can't recall" as a second escape when the box already takes 0, so two chips do overlapping work.
screens.why5: It asks about wasted cluster capacity in plain operator terms and nothing of the product or the founder's labels for people reaches me.
screens.why6: The question says well, but "A percent of GPU hours last month, or a low and a high; none is 0" is a clipped instruction that sounds odd heard once.
screens.instead: Last month, about what share of your cluster's allocated GPU hours sat idle? A percent, or say I can't recall.

screens.why1: Right after the idea card and the question about reserved-but-unused GPU hours, asking what it would be worth to me per month is the obvious next step for the person who pays for cluster tools.
screens.why2: Per month, per cluster, in dollars is how I already think about scheduler, monitoring and licence spend, so I can answer it on first reading.
screens.why3: I sign off on software for the cluster and know what we pay for comparable tools, so I can price this from my own budget rather than guessing.
screens.why4: The bands are distinct and cover the range for a cluster of 100 or more GPUs, 'I wouldn't pay for this' is a real floor, and 'I can't say' is the right escape.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's idea as an operator buying predicted job resource needs per cluster, and nothing beyond the card's own words leaks to me.
screens.why6: The two-step ladder reads well and is easy to hold, but 'Or say you can't say' trips the ear and sounds like a riddle rather than an escape.
screens.instead: What would Expanse be worth to you a month, per cluster? Under $10,000; $10,000 to under $25,000; $25,000 or more; or you wouldn't pay for this. Or tell me you're not sure.

screens.why1: Right after I named a monthly price, asking where that money would actually come from is the natural next question for the person who pays for cluster software.
screens.why2: Budget line, signed off and other spending are how I talk about funding the cluster, so I can answer on first read.
screens.why3: I hold the cluster's budget and know whether we have an existing software line, would need a new allocation approved, or would cut something else.
screens.why4: On a national or shared cluster the money often comes from a grant or allocation, or from charging it back to user groups, and neither is offered; 'There was no budget for it' is past tense in a hypothetical, and 'signed off' is missing 'on'.
screens.why5: It names Expanse only as the idea already shown and repeats my own price back, with nothing of the founder's plan or terms leaking.
screens.why6: Four short options are easy to hold, but the closing 'Or say you can't say' trips when heard, and 'there was no budget' jars in a would-question.
screens.instead: Think of the price you just gave. If you went ahead at that, where would the money come from? A budget line we already have; a new budget someone would sign off on; a grant or allocation; charged back to user groups; or taken from other spending. Or: I can't say.

screens.why1: Right after I said what it's worth and where the money comes from, asking who signs off on that spend is the natural next step.
screens.why2: It reads cleanly, but on a national shared cluster the person above me is the center director or the allocation board, not a department head, so I have to translate that word.
screens.why3: I know exactly who signs off on software spend for the cluster, so I can answer from my own work.
screens.why4: The options cover the real cases, but leading with No-department-head before Yes is an odd order, and department head blurs into someone else's decision when my approver is a director or a board.
screens.why5: Taking about $10,000 from my $10,000 to $25,000 band is fair, but department head drifts toward a university department rather than the shared-cluster operator the founder means.
screens.why6: It says well overall, but the four long No-led options are a lot to hold, and Or say you can't say is clumsy to hear.
screens.instead: Could you sign off on about $10,000 a month for the cluster yourself, or would someone above you have to agree? Options: Yes, I could sign off myself · No, my director would have to agree · No, a committee or board would decide · No, it's someone else's budget; escape: I can't say

screens.why1: After price, payer and sign-off, asking how long security would take to clear an agent on our nodes is exactly the next thing that stalls a purchase like this.
screens.why2: Plain enough to a cluster operator, but 'an agent on every node' is a little clipped and 'before it went through' needs a second read to see it means approval.
screens.why3: I know how long our security team takes to clear a daemon going onto every compute node, so I can answer from experience.
screens.why4: The duration bands are distinct and cover the range, 'It wouldn't be needed' fits clusters with no such review, and 'I can't tell' is the right escape.
screens.why5: It still means the founder's step, but 'agent on every node' hints at the product's design and the stem drops the product's name, which reads a little drifted.
screens.why6: One short question, four options then a two-way follow-up, and one escape said last, all easy to hold by ear.
screens.instead: If you bought Expanse, how long would security take to approve putting its software on every node? Under 6 weeks; 6 weeks to 3 months; over 3 months; or it wouldn't be needed. Or say you can't tell.

screens.why1: I just said the security review of an agent on every node would take months, so asking what would eat that time is the obvious next thing.
screens.why2: Plain words I'd use myself; I can answer it straight off.
screens.why3: I know exactly what drags: infosec sign-off on a privileged daemon on every compute node, change control on the scheduler, and procurement paperwork.
screens.why4: A box to type in, no options.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's meaning, asking what slows the purchase, and nothing leaks beyond the product name I've already seen on the idea card.
screens.why6: One short question of nine words, easy to hear once and answer aloud.

screens.why1: After price, sign-off and security review, asking whether I'd actually trial it on my cluster is the obvious last step.
screens.why2: I can follow it, but I'd call it a utilization audit or a pilot, and 'waste measurement' doesn't tell me what gets installed on my nodes for those two weeks.
screens.why3: Whether a trial runs on the cluster is my call, so I can answer from what I'd actually do.
screens.why4: There's a 'Probably not' with no 'Probably yes' to match it, so a cautious yes has nowhere to go except the full yes.
screens.why5: 'Waste measurement' sounds like the vendor's pitch for the trial rather than my words, though it doesn't misstate the idea.
screens.why6: It's one short question with three options that are easy to hold, even if the yes option repeats the stem.
screens.instead: If it were ready today, would you run a two-week trial of Expanse on one cluster to measure unused GPU hours, or not? Yes, I'd run it · Probably yes · Probably not · No
